query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A two‐step surface treatment on Ti–6Al–4V—first, low‐temperature plasma nitriding in an NH3–N2 (1:2) atmosphere to form a robust Ti–N compound layer, and second, a controlled low-energy laser surface texturing to generate microscopic dimples—will synergistically increase the surface hardness and reduce the friction coefficient, thereby markedly enhancing wear resistance compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Ti–6Al–4V alloy with a Widmanstätten-type (or equiaxed) microstructure in its as-received or annealed state.
generation.intervention: Apply plasma nitriding at around 750°C for 4 hours using an NH3–N2 (1:2) gas mixture to develop a TiN/Ti2N layer with a deep diffusion zone, followed by a low-energy laser surface texturing process to create a regular array of micro-dimples.
generation.conditions: Under room-temperature dry sliding wear tests with moderate loads (e.g., around 5–8 N) and comparable test durations to prior studies; the effect is expected during both low-cycle and high-cycle wear conditions relevant to structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dual-layer structure: an outer, hard nitride compound layer (TiN and Ti2N) with underlying nitrogen-diffused support combined with engineered micro-dimples that effectively lower the real area of contact and act as debris traps.
generation.mechanism: Plasma nitriding increases surface hardness and induces beneficial compressive residual stresses by generating hard Ti–N phases, thereby inhibiting dislocation motion and crack initiation. The subsequent laser surface texturing reduces effective contact area and friction by creating micro-reservoirs for wear debris, which minimizes abrasive wear and delays detrimental crack growth.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in surface hardness by roughly 200–300% compared to the untreated alloy and a significant reduction in the wear rate (potentially doubling the wear life) owing to both the high mechanical strength of the nitride layer and the lower friction provided by the textured morphology.
generation.baseline: The untreated Ti–6Al–4V alloy, which typically shows lower hardness (around 400–450 HV) and higher wear rates under similar test conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvements are anticipated for structural components under moderate-to-high contact stress in dry or lightly lubricated environments; however, if the nitriding process overly increases brittleness or if the texturing parameters are not optimized, the favorable effects might be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extrapolates observations from separate studies on plasma nitriding (e.g., enhanced hardness and compressive stress effects in PMC6384831) and on surface texturing (e.g., friction reduction in PMC6356806) to a combined treatment on a structural Ti alloy. The precise quantitative synergy between the two treatments and the optimal texturing design remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three groups of Ti–6Al–4V samples: (1) untreated, (2) plasma nitrided only (using the specified 750°C, 4 h, NH3–N2 (1:2) process), and (3) plasma nitrided followed by controlled laser surface texturing. Conduct standardized room-temperature dry sliding wear tests (e.g., with an 8 N load for a defined sliding distance). Measure surface hardness, friction coefficient, and wear volume for each group.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/Nm or weight loss measurements)
Coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Surface morphology and microstructural integrity (via SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined treatment (nitriding + texturing) does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than 50% reduction in wear rate and less than a 1.5× increase in hardness) over the plasma-nitrided only samples, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The growth of the Ti-N compound layer was enhanced by the use of an NH3-N2 mixture during the plasma nitriding of the Ti6Al4V alloy. After nitriding at 750 °C for 4 h in an NH3-N2 (1:2) atmosphere, a Ti-N compound layer approximately 2 μm thick was formed on the Ti6Al4V alloy. The Ti-N compound layers are typically much harder than the titanium alloy substrate. In comparison to the un-nitrided titanium alloy, samples nitrided in an NH3-N2 mixture exhibited the complete elimination of stick–tear and plowing wear throughout the duration of the test, resulting in undetectable wear loss when in contact with bearing steel. The oxide layer formed on the wear track by the transfer of material from the counterpart steel ball reduced the average friction coefficient from approximately 0.55 to 0.30 under an 8N load. The formation of the Ti-N layer not only enhances the hardness and wear resistance of the titanium alloy but also increases its corrosion resistance.

Increased fatigue life of the plasma nitrided specimens in tests at higher stresses can be attributed to compressive residual stress in the nitride layers and in the nitrogen diffusion zone, thereby inhibiting crack nucleation at the alloy surface. This is in agreement with another study by Rodriguez et al. []. According to Farokhzadeh et al. [], the nitride layer reduces the extent of brittle failure on the specimen surface while the diffusion zone provides mechanical support. As per the study of Morita et al [], the formation of these layers after plasma nitriding increases the surface hardness of the alloy, which in turn increases the resistance to movement of dislocations and, as a consequence, increases the fatigue strength of the alloy. Rocha [], reported that delay in crack nucleation in plasma nitrided specimens is due to the difference in the Young modulus between the titanium alloy matrix (100 GPa) and the titanium nitrides formed on the plasma nitride surface (400 GPa). When high stresses are applied to the fragile nitride layer, it causes the nucleation and the growth of a crack in this layer.
